I spent two weeks chasing a single ghost checkout bug on STRAYED.

We were setting up our custom payment flow and the checkout was lagging. Users would hit pay, get their money deducted, but the order confirmation screen would just hang. Tbh, it was incredibly frustrating because on paper, everything looked perfectly clean.

The issue turned out to be how we handled Razorpay webhooks. The webhook was triggering a confirmation email before the local database write fully completed. This caused a weird race condition that kept mobile users staring at a spinning loader.

To fix it, we refactored our state machine to prioritize optimistic UI updates. Now, the client assumes success immediately after the gateway callback, while a silent database query handles any delays in the background. Latency dropped to almost zero.

It made me realize how much of good UX is just hiding backend latency from the user.

When you add an item to your cart on Amazon, the UI updates instantly. There is no spinner, no lag, and no waiting for a server confirmation.

If the server request fails for some rare reason, we gracefully roll back the UI state and show a quick notification. But 99% of the time, the user experiences an instant, snappy transition.

I spent three days trying to fix a ghost database connection timeout. 

Every time our traffic spiked past a few hundred concurrent users, our database connection pool would just stop responding. My initial instinct was to blame the VPS provider and look for a bigger server instance to throw at the problem. 

It turned out to be a classic connection leak in our Node.js middleware. I was opening a new database client for every single incoming request but failing to release it back to the pool once the operation finished. The server was effectively hitting a dead end because the pool was full of abandoned connections. 

I swapped the manual connection management for a proper persistent pool configuration and wrapped the queries in a try-finally block. The resource consumption dropped by sixty percent instantly, and the site stopped hanging under load. 

We often look for complex infrastructure solutions when the bottleneck is usually a simple case of improper resource handling in our own code.
